claim: Peptidoglycan (PG) is a giant macromolecule that completely surrounds bacterial cells and prevents lysis in hypo-osmotic environments.
source: Peptidoglycan (PG) is a giant macromolecule that completely surrounds bacterial cells and prevents lysis in hypo-osmotic environments.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rojas et al., 2018 and established scientific knowledge about peptidoglycan function.

claim: The peptidoglycan net-like macromolecule is made of glycan strands linked to each other by two types of transpeptidases that form either 4→3 (PBPs) or 3→3 (LDTs) cross-links.
source: This net-like macromolecule is made of glycan strands linked to each other by two types of transpeptidases that form either 4→3 (PBPs) or 3→3 (LDTs) cross-links.
evidence: Supported by citation to Glauner et al., 1988 and established knowledge of peptidoglycan structure.

claim: PG polymerization operates according to different modes for the formation of the septum and of the lateral cell walls.
source: We showed that PG polymerization operates according to different modes for the formation of the septum and of the lateral cell walls, as well as for bacterial growth in the presence or absence of β-lactams in engineered strains that can exclusively rely on LDTs for PG cross-linking when drugs are present.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous work (Atze et al., 2022) where this was demonstrated.

claim: Lpp and disaccharide-peptide subunits are independently incorporated into the expanding lateral cell walls.
source: We find that Lpp and disaccharide-peptide subunits are independently incorporated into the expanding lateral cell walls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from isotope labeling and mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Newly synthesized septum PG appears to contain small amounts of tethered Lpp.
source: Newly synthesized septum PG appears to contain small amounts of tethered Lpp.
evidence: Inferred from the low abundance of new→new Tri→KR isotopologues at early time points as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LDTs mediate intense shuffling of Lpp between PG stems leading to a dynamic equilibrium between the PG-tethered and free forms of Lpp.
source: LDTs did mediate intense shuffling of Lpp between PG stems leading to a dynamic equilibrium between the PG-tethered and free forms of Lpp.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing BW25113 and ΔyafK mutant strains shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PBPs and LDTs contain different catalytic nucleophiles (Ser versus Cys) and use different stem peptides as the acyl donor substrate (pentapeptide versus tetrapeptide).
source: PBPs and LDTs contain different catalytic nucleophiles (Ser versus Cys) and use different stem peptides as the acyl donor substrate (pentapeptide versus tetrapeptide) (Figure 1C; Mainardi et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mainardi et al., 2005 and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: LDTs forming 3→3 cross-links are unessential enzymes.
source: LDTs forming 3→3 cross-links are unessential enzymes (Magnet et al., 2008), which can participate in PG maintenance (Morè et al., 2019) and in β-lactam resistance acquired in vitro (Voedts et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Magnet et al., 2008, Morè et al., 2019, and Voedts et al., 2022.

claim: The LDT family includes enzymes that catalyze the tethering of Lpp to PG (ErfK, Ybis, and YcfS).
source: The LDT family includes additional enzymes (Figure 1C) that catalyze either the tethering of Lpp to PG (ErfK, Ybis, and YcfS) (Magnet et al., 2008) or the hydrolysis of the resulting covalent link (YafK) (Bahadur et al., 2021; Winkle et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Magnet et al., 2008 and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: YafK catalyzes the hydrolysis of the PG→Lpp covalent link.
source: The LDT family includes additional enzymes (Figure 1C) that catalyze either the tethering of Lpp to PG (ErfK, Ybis, and YcfS) (Magnet et al., 2008) or the hydrolysis of the resulting covalent link (YafK) (Bahadur et al., 2021; Winkle et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bahadur et al., 2021 and Winkle et al., 2021, and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Lpp is the most abundant lipoprotein with 10^6 copies per cell.
source: Lpp is the most abundant lipoprotein (106 copies per cell), about one-third of which is attached to PG.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Lpp abundance in E. coli.

claim: About one-third of Lpp is attached to PG.
source: Lpp is the most abundant lipoprotein (106 copies per cell), about one-third of which is attached to PG.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about Lpp distribution.

claim: The dense connection between the PG and the outer membrane is thought to stabilize the bacterial envelope.
source: This dense connection between the PG and the outer membrane (OM) is thought to stabilize the bacterial envelope because mutants deficient in the tethering of Lpp to PG are viable but display increased vesiculation and lethal susceptibility to EDTA (Sanders and Pavelka, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanders and Pavelka, 2013 showing phenotypes of mutants lacking Lpp-PG tethering.

claim: Mutants deficient in the tethering of Lpp to PG are viable but display increased vesiculation and lethal susceptibility to EDTA.
source: This dense connection between the PG and the outer membrane (OM) is thought to stabilize the bacterial envelope because mutants deficient in the tethering of Lpp to PG are viable but display increased vesiculation and lethal susceptibility to EDTA (Sanders and Pavelka, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanders and Pavelka, 2013.

claim: Lpp controls the distance between the inner and outer membranes.
source: In addition, Lpp controls the distance between the inner (IM) and outer membranes, a structural feature that is critical for sensing stresses that affect the bacterial envelope (Asmar et al., 2017; Mathelié-Guinlet et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Asmar et al., 2017 and Mathelié-Guinlet et al., 2020.

claim: The distance between the inner and outer membranes is critical for sensing stresses that affect the bacterial envelope.
source: In addition, Lpp controls the distance between the inner (IM) and outer membranes, a structural feature that is critical for sensing stresses that affect the bacterial envelope (Asmar et al., 2017; Mathelié-Guinlet et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Asmar et al., 2017 and Mathelié-Guinlet et al., 2020.

claim: The enzymatic activity of YafK was established by incubating PG with purified YafK and detecting the products of the hydrolysis of the PG→Lpp bonds.
source: The enzymatic activity of YafK was established by incubating PG with purified YafK and detecting the products of the hydrolysis of the PG→Lpp bonds (Bahadur et al., 2021; Winkle et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bahadur et al., 2021 and Winkle et al., 2021.

claim: The deletion of yafK was not associated with any decrease in the overall Lpp-to-PG tethering in the absence of stress.
source: Intriguingly, the deletion of yafK was not associated with any decrease in the overall Lpp-to-PG tethering in the absence of stress (Bahadur et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bahadur et al., 2021.

claim: Tethering of Lpp to PG generates Tri→KR isotopologues containing light and heavy moieties at both the donor (tripeptide) and acceptor (Lpp) positions.
source: This analysis revealed that tethering of Lpp to PG did generate Tri→KR isotopologues containing light and heavy moieties at both the donor (tripeptide) and acceptor (Lpp) positions.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Tri→KR isotopologues of the new→new type were only detected at late times of the kinetics, when light tetrapeptide stems became abundant in the PG.
source: Indeed, this would have resulted in the linking of newly synthesized Lpp to newly synthesized stem peptide in lipid II, thus leading to the formation of Tri→KR isotopologues of the new→new type, which were only detected at late times of the kinetics, when light tetrapeptide stems became abundant in the PG (Figure 3A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The low abundance of Tri→KR isotopologues of the new→new type at early times indicates that Lpp is not preferentially incorporated at locations in which new disaccharide-peptide subunits are incorporated into the expanding PG.
source: The low abundance of Tri→KR isotopologues of the new→new type at early times of the kinetics also indicates that Lpp is not preferentially incorporated at locations in which new disaccharide-peptide subunits are incorporated into the expanding PG.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The tethering of Lpp to PG and the incorporation of newly synthesized subunits are spatially independent.
source: Thus, the tethering of Lpp to PG and the incorporation of newly synthesized subunits are spatially independent.
evidence: Inferred from the low abundance of new→new isotopologues at early time points shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The mode of insertion of PG subunits into the expanding PG is different in the side walls and in the septum.
source: The mode of insertion of PG subunits into the expanding PG is different in the side walls and in the septum (de Jonge et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to de Jonge et al., 1989.

claim: One-at-a-time insertion of newly synthesized glycan strands into the side walls leads to a mosaic of new and old subunits gradually enriched in new subunits.
source: One-at-a-time insertion of newly synthesized glycan strands into the side walls leads to a mosaic of new and old subunits gradually enriched in new subunits.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peptidoglycan synthesis in lateral walls, supported by citation to de Jonge et al., 1989.

claim: The septum mainly consists of newly synthesized PG subunits.
source: In contrast, the septum mainly consists of newly synthesized PG subunits.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peptidoglycan synthesis in the septum, supported by citation to de Jonge et al., 1989.

claim: Lpp might be incorporated in very limited amounts into nascent septal PG.
source: The low abundance of new→new Tri→KR isotopologues at early time points (Figure 3A) thus suggests that Lpp might be incorporated in very limited amounts into nascent septal PG.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: YafK is actively hydrolyzing tripeptide→Lpp bonds.
source: The decrease in the relative abundance of old→old isotopologues was slower in the absence of YafK (Figure 3B), thus establishing that YafK is actively hydrolyzing tripeptide→Lpp bonds.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing BW25113 and ΔyafK mutant shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At the beginning of the kinetics (0–25min), the absence of YafK had little impact on the relative abundance of old→new isotopologues.
source: At the beginning of the kinetics (0–25min), the absence of YafK had little impact on the relative abundance of old→new isotopologues (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The bulk of the PG contains old tetrapeptide stems that act as donors in the transpeptidation reaction at early time points.
source: This is expected since the bulk of the PG contains old tetrapeptide stems that act as donors in the transpeptidation reaction, thus leading to the tethering of newly synthesized Lpp to old PG.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design and the kinetics of isotope replacement.

claim: The proportion of old→new isotopologues levels off earlier in the BW25113 strain than in the ΔyafK mutant.
source: At later times, the proportion of old→new isotopologues levels off earlier in the BW25113 strain than in the ΔyafK mutant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Hydrolysis of old→new isotopologues by YafK generates light Lpp molecules that can be cross-linked to light tetrapeptide donor stems.
source: This may be accounted for by the hydrolysis of old→new isotopologues by YafK, thus generating light Lpp molecules that can be cross-linked to light tetrapeptide donor stems, the abundance of which increases after the medium switch.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and the known enzymatic activity of YafK.

claim: The larger relative abundance of new→old isotopologues in the ΔyafK mutant provides an indication that hydrolysis of tripeptide→Lpp bonds by YafK results in the shuffling of Lpp between PG stem peptides.
source: Thus, the larger relative abundance of new→old isotopologues in the ΔyafK mutant provides a first indication that hydrolysis of tripeptide→Lpp bonds by YafK results in the shuffling of Lpp between PG stem peptides.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data comparing BW25113 and ΔyafK mutant shown in Figure 3.

claim: The relative abundance of new→old isotopologues was higher in the BW25113 strain than in the ΔyafK mutant at all incubation times.
source: The relative abundance of new→old isotopologues was higher in the BW25113 strain than in the ΔyafK mutant at all incubation times (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The heavy Lpp molecules used for the formation of new→old isotopologues originate both from the old pool of free Lpp and from the YafK-mediated hydrolysis of old→old isotopologues.
source: The heavy Lpp molecules used for the formation of these isotopologues are expected to originate both from the old pool of free Lpp and from the YafK-mediated hydrolysis of old→old isotopologues.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design and the known enzymatic activity of YafK.

claim: The reduction in the relative abundance of new→old isotopologues upon deletion of yafK indicates that hydrolysis of tripeptide→Lpp bonds by YafK results in the shuffling of Lpp between PG stem peptides.
source: Thus, the reduction in the relative abundance of new→old isotopologues upon deletion of yafK additionally indicates that hydrolysis of tripeptide→Lpp bonds by YafK results in the shuffling of Lpp between PG stem peptides.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At least 50% of the tripeptide→Lpp bonds are hydrolyzed in one generation.
source: At least 50% of the tripeptide→Lpp bonds are hydrolyzed in one generation
evidence: Calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D comparing BW25113 and ΔyafK mutant.

claim: The twofold decrease in the relative abundance of old→old isotopologues over the course of one generation in the absence of YafK can be fully accounted for by the synthesis of new PG stem peptides and Lpp molecules.
source: The twofold decrease in the relative abundance of old→old isotopologues over the course of one generation, as observed in the absence of YafK (Figure 3B), can be fully accounted for by the synthesis of new PG stem peptides and Lpp molecules.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3B and theoretical considerations about bacterial growth.

claim: There was no detectable loss of old→old isotopologues in the ΔyafK strain.
source: Thus, there was no detectable loss of old→old isotopologues in the ΔyafK strain.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relative abundance of old Lpp present in both the old→old and new→old isotopologues decreased twofold in 60 min both in the BW25113 strain and in the ΔyafK mutant.
source: Furthermore, the relative abundance of old Lpp present in both the old→old and new→old isotopologues decreased twofold in 60 min both in the BW25113 strain and in the ΔyafK mutant (Figure 4A and B and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Hydrolysis of tripeptide→Lpp bonds by YafK was not associated with any proteolytic degradation of the released Lpp.
source: This implies that hydrolysis of tripeptide→Lpp bonds by YafK was not associated with any proteolytic degradation of the released Lpp.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that old Lpp decreased twofold in both strains, as shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The relative abundance of old tripeptide stems present in both the old→old and old→new isotopologues decreased more rapidly in the BW25113 strain than in the ΔyafK mutant (four versus twofold in 60 min).
source: In contrast, the relative abundance of old tripeptide stems present in both the old→old and old→new isotopologues decreased more rapidly in the BW25113 strain than in the ΔyafK mutant (four versus twofold in 60 min; Figure 4C and D, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Hydrolysis of the Tri→KR bond by YafK resulted in a twofold decrease in the relative abundance of old tripeptide stems in old→old and old→new isotopologues.
source: Thus, hydrolysis of the Tri→KR bond by YafK resulted in a twofold decrease in the relative abundance of old tripeptide stems in these isotopologues, providing an estimate of 50% for the proportion of tripeptide→Lpp bonds hydrolyzed in one generation.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Old Lpp released by YafK can be cross-linked to a donor containing an old tetrapeptide stem, a reaction that regenerates old→old and old→new isotopologues.
source: This is a low estimate since old Lpp released by YafK can be cross-linked to a donor containing an old tetrapeptide stem, a reaction that regenerates old→old and old→new isotopologues.
evidence: Inferred from the known enzymatic activities of LDTs and the experimental observations.

claim: Lpp is not tethered to PG precursors prior to their polymerization.
source: Here, we show that Lpp is not tethered to PG precursors prior to their polymerization, as is the case for the reaction catalyzed by sortases in Gram-positive bacteria (Dramsi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3, and contrasted with sortase mechanism cited from Dramsi et al., 2008.

claim: In Gram-positive bacteria, proteins are tethered to PG by sortases that use lipid II as the acceptor of the transpeptidation reaction.
source: In Gram-positive bacteria, proteins are tethered to PG by sortases that use lipid II as the acceptor of the transpeptidation reaction (Dramsi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dramsi et al., 2008.

claim: Lpp is incorporated into the expanding lateral cell walls independently from their sites of expansion.
source: Instead, Lpp is incorporated into the expanding lateral cell walls independently from their sites of expansion.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing spatial independence of Lpp tethering and subunit incorporation.

claim: The free form of Lpp faces the bacterial surfaces.
source: The free form of Lpp faces the bacterial surfaces raising the possibility that pools of free and PG-tethered Lpp might not be in dynamic equilibrium (Asmar and Collet, 2018).
evidence: Based on structural knowledge of Lpp orientation, with citation to Asmar and Collet, 2018.

claim: Pools of free and PG-tethered Lpp are in dynamic equilibrium.
source: This is not the case because new→old isotopologues are formed in the absence of YafK (Figure 3), showing that existing (old) Lpp is translocated from the outer leaflet of the OM to the periplasm and tethered to neo-synthesized PG subunits.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 demonstrating formation of new→old isotopologues in ΔyafK mutant.

claim: Existing (old) Lpp is translocated from the outer leaflet of the OM to the periplasm and tethered to neo-synthesized PG subunits.
source: This is not the case because new→old isotopologues are formed in the absence of YafK (Figure 3), showing that existing (old) Lpp is translocated from the outer leaflet of the OM to the periplasm and tethered to neo-synthesized PG subunits.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lpp tethered to PG is expected to prevent OM budding.
source: Since Lpp tethered to PG is expected to prevent OM budding, it has been proposed that vesicles are released from OM domains lacking PG-tethered Lpp (Schwechheimer et al., 2014; McMillan and Kuehn, 2021).
evidence: Based on inference from structural constraints and supported by citations to Schwechheimer et al., 2014 and McMillan and Kuehn, 2021.

claim: Vesicles are released from OM domains lacking PG-tethered Lpp.
source: Since Lpp tethered to PG is expected to prevent OM budding, it has been proposed that vesicles are released from OM domains lacking PG-tethered Lpp (Schwechheimer et al., 2014; McMillan and Kuehn, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwechheimer et al., 2014 and McMillan and Kuehn, 2021.

claim: The dynamic equilibrium between free and PG-tethered Lpp may be physiologically relevant to spatially control the formation of OM vesicles.
source: The dynamic equilibrium between free and PG-tethered Lpp may, therefore, be physiologically relevant to spatially control the formation of OM vesicles, and thereby, their periplasmic content.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: The E. coli BW25113 strain produces the full complement of six L,D-transpeptidases.
source: To investigate the mode of tethering of the Braun lipoprotein to PG, the E. coli BW25113 strain, which produces the full complement of six L,D-transpeptidases, and its derivative obtained by deletion of the yafK gene, were grown in minimal medium containing [13C]glucose and [15N]ammonium chloride to obtain fully labeled PG all procedures are described in details in Atze et al., 2022.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the BW25113 strain genotype.

claim: Bacteria were grown in minimal medium containing [13C]glucose and [15N]ammonium chloride to obtain fully labeled PG.
source: To investigate the mode of tethering of the Braun lipoprotein to PG, the E. coli BW25113 strain, which produces the full complement of six L,D-transpeptidases, and its derivative obtained by deletion of the yafK gene, were grown in minimal medium containing [13C]glucose and [15N]ammonium chloride to obtain fully labeled PG all procedures are described in details in Atze et al., 2022.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used, with reference to detailed procedures in Atze et al., 2022.

claim: At an optical density of 0.4 at 600 nm, bacteria were centrifuged and resuspended in a minimal medium containing light isotopes of carbon and nitrogen for a continued incubation of 60 min corresponding to one generation.
source: At an optical density of 0.4 at 600 nm, bacteria were centrifuged, and resuspended in a minimal medium with the same chemical composition but containing the light isotopes of carbon and nitrogen ([12C] and [14N]) for a continued incubation of 60 min corresponding to one generation.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used.

claim: The PG macromolecule was extracted from culture samples by the hot SDS procedure, digested with pronase and trypsin, and treated with muramidases.
source: The PG macromolecule was extracted from these culture samples by the hot SDS procedure, digested with pronase and trypsin, and treated with muramidase's, which cleave the β-glycosidic bond connecting MurNAc to GlcNAc residues.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used.

claim: Muramidases cleave the β-glycosidic bond connecting MurNAc to GlcNAc residues.
source: The PG macromolecule was extracted from these culture samples by the hot SDS procedure, digested with pronase and trypsin, and treated with muramidase's, which cleave the β-glycosidic bond connecting MurNAc to GlcNAc residues.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of muramidase enzymatic activity.

claim: Treatment of PG with pronase, trypsin, and muramidases led to the release of soluble disaccharide-peptide fragments (muropeptides).
source: This procedure led to the release of soluble disaccharide-peptide fragments (muropeptides) that were reduced with sodium borohydride (conversion of MurNAc to muramitol residues) and purified by rpHPLC.
evidence: Describes the experimental method and its results.

claim: Muropeptides were reduced with sodium borohydride resulting in conversion of MurNAc to muramitol residues.
source: This procedure led to the release of soluble disaccharide-peptide fragments (muropeptides) that were reduced with sodium borohydride (conversion of MurNAc to muramitol residues) and purified by rpHPLC.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used.

claim: The isotopic compositions of the Tri→KR isotopologues was determined by mass spectrometry and tandem mass spectrometry.
source: The isotopic compositions of the Tri→KR isotopologues was determined by mass spectrometry and tandem mass spectrometry.
evidence: Describes the analytical method used, with results shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The envelope of gram-negative bacteria contains two membranes.
source: The envelope of gram-negative bacteria contains two membranes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of gram-negative bacterial cell envelope structure, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The inner membrane is made of phospholipids.
source: The inner membrane (IM) is made of phospholipids.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of bacterial membrane composition, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The outer membrane is asymmetric, with phospholipids in the inner leaflet and lipopolysaccharides (LPS) in the outer leaflet.
source: The outer membrane (OM) is asymmetric, with phospholipids in the inner leaflet and lipopolysaccharides (LPS) in the outer leaflet.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of outer membrane structure, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The peptidoglycan is located in the periplasmic space delimited by the IM and the OM.
source: The peptidoglycan (PG) is located in the periplasmic space delimited by the IM and the OM.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of bacterial cell envelope structure, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The PG consists of glycan chains linked to each other by short peptides.
source: The PG consists of glycan chains linked to each other by short peptides.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peptidoglycan structure, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The glycan chains consist of alternating β1→4-linked N-acetyl-glucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetyl muramic acid (MurNAc) residues.
source: The glycan chains consist of alternating β1→4-linked N-acetyl-glucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetyl muramic acid (MurNAc) residues.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peptidoglycan structure, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The sequence of the stem peptide linked to the D-lactoyl group of MurNAc, as assembled in the cytoplasm, is L-Ala1-D-iGlu2-DAP3-D-Ala4-D-Ala5.
source: The sequence of the stem peptide linked to the D-lactoyl group of MurNAc, as assembled in the cytoplasm, is L-Ala1-D-iGlu2-DAP3-D-Ala4-D-Ala5, in which DAP is a diaminopimelyl residue.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peptidoglycan precursor structure, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Polymerization of the disaccharide-pentapeptide subunit by glycosyltransferases results in linear glycan strands that are inserted into the expanding PG network by the combined actions of space-making hydrolases and transpeptidases.
source: Polymerization of this disaccharide-pentapeptide subunit by glycosyltransferases results in linear glycan strands that are inserted into the expanding PG network by the combined actions of space-making hydrolases and transpeptidases.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peptidoglycan biosynthesis, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The majority of the cross-links connecting D-Ala4 of a donor stem peptide to DAP3 of an acceptor stem peptide (4→3 cross-links) are made by D,D-transpeptidases belonging to the penicillin-binding protein (PBP) family.
source: The majority of the cross-links connecting D-Ala4 of a donor stem peptide to DAP3 of an acceptor stem peptide (4→3 cross-links) are made by D,D-transpeptidases belonging to the penicillin-binding protein (PBP) family that are the essential targets of β-lactam antibiotics.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peptidoglycan cross-linking, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: PBPs are the essential targets of β-lactam antibiotics.
source: The majority of the cross-links connecting D-Ala4 of a donor stem peptide to DAP3 of an acceptor stem peptide (4→3 cross-links) are made by D,D-transpeptidases belonging to the penicillin-binding protein (PBP) family that are the essential targets of β-lactam antibiotics.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of β-lactam antibiotic mechanism of action.

claim: The Braun lipoprotein provides a link between the OM and the PG since its C-terminus is covalently bound to DAP residues.
source: The Braun lipoprotein (Lpp) provides a link between the OM and the PG since its C-terminus is covalently bound to DAP residues (panel C), whereas its N-terminal Cys residue carries three alkyl chains, one of which is carried by the amino group of the C-terminal Cys residue and the other two by a glycerol moiety linked to the sulfhydryl of that residue by a thioether bond.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Lpp structure and function, illustrated in Figure 1A and 1C.

claim: The N-terminal Cys residue of Lpp carries three alkyl chains.
source: The Braun lipoprotein (Lpp) provides a link between the OM and the PG since its C-terminus is covalently bound to DAP residues (panel C), whereas its N-terminal Cys residue carries three alkyl chains, one of which is carried by the amino group of the C-terminal Cys residue and the other two by a glycerol moiety linked to the sulfhydryl of that residue by a thioether bond.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lipoprotein structure.

claim: The alkyl chains of Lpp are inserted into the inner leaflet of the OM in the PG-tethered form or into the outer leaflet in the free form facing the bacterial cell surface.
source: These alkyl chains are inserted into the inner leaflet of the OM (PG-tethered form of Lpp) or into the outer leaflet of that membrane (free form of Lpp facing the bacterial cell surface).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Lpp topology, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In E. coli, the LDT protein family includes six paralogues.
source: In E. coli, the LDT protein family includes six paralogues that catalyze (i) the formation of 3→3 cross-links (YcbB and YnhG), (ii) the covalent anchoring of Lpp to PG (Ybis, YcfS, and ErfK), and (iii) the hydrolysis of the resulting PG→Lpp bond (YafK).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of E. coli LDT family, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: YcbB and YnhG catalyze the formation of 3→3 cross-links.
source: In E. coli, the LDT protein family includes six paralogues that catalyze (i) the formation of 3→3 cross-links (YcbB and YnhG), (ii) the covalent anchoring of Lpp to PG (Ybis, YcfS, and ErfK), and (iii) the hydrolysis of the resulting PG→Lpp bond (YafK).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of LDT enzyme activities, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Formation of the 3→3 and PG→Lpp bonds involves a common catalytic intermediate resulting from the nucleophilic attack of the DAP3-D-Ala4 bond of an acyl-donor tetrapeptide stem by the active Cys residue of the LDTs.
source: Formation of the 3→3 and PG→Lpp bonds involves a common catalytic intermediate resulting from the nucleophilic attack of the DAP3-D-Ala4 bond of an acyl-donor tetrapeptide stem by the active Cys residue of the LDTs, the release of D-Ala4, and the formation of a D-Ala4-Cys thioester bond.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of LDT catalytic mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: For the formation of a 3→3 cross-link, the side-chain amino group of DAP at the third position of an acyl acceptor stem reacts with the acyl-enzyme.
source: For the formation of a 3→3 cross-link, the side-chain amino group of DAP at the third position of an acyl acceptor stem reacts with the acyl-enzyme.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of LDT catalytic mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: For the formation of a PG→Lpp bond, the side-chain of the C-terminal Lys residue of Lpp (at position 58) reacts with the acyl-enzyme.
source: For the formation of a PG→Lpp bond, the side-chain of the C-terminal Lys residue of Lpp (at position 58) reacts with the acyl-enzyme.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Lpp-PG tethering mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1C.
